subject: Extremely high slope estimate for one covariate

messages.author: 0707d026c588639b
messages.subject: Extremely high slope estimate for one covariate
parts:
Hi guys,

I was modeling on some bird data, and I found a extremely high slope estimate with my model, which looks like this:


Other slope estimates are about +-1, but the genome_heterozygosity is 20-40. I don't know what happened.

In the practice of modeling, each time I put one variate into the model, and the variate is added only if the wAIC decrease by 2 or more.

Besides, will it be a normalization or standerization problem?

My code:
```
#### reasonable values for mesh
minME<-10;maxME<-50;co<-3;minOS<-30;maxOS<-50

##make mesh
mesh6<-inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain=data1[,c("Lon","Lat")], max.edge = c(minME, maxME), cutoff = co, offset = c(minOS, maxOS))
plot(mesh6)
points(data1[,c("Lon","Lat")])

####The SPDE model is defined with following priors 
sig0 = 1;rho0 = 1
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh6, alpha=2, prior.pc.rho = c(rho0, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(sig0, 0.5))

###projector matrix for known
A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh6, loc = as.matrix(data1[,c("Lon","Lat")]))

###make index for spatial field
s.index<-inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field",n.spde=spde$n.spde)

##and the stack data is defined
stk.est <- inla.stack(data=list(y=log(data1$ys+1)),
                      A=list(A,1), 
                      effects=list(c(s.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                                   list(data1[,4:ncol(data1)])),
                      tag='est')

##for number of trials in binomial
ntt=rep(1,nrow(data1))

fam1="gaussian" 

#####Notice: here I put each covariate into a variate in R, named from "gr01" to "gr99"###
ori<-"y ~ 0 + Intercept"
ori1<-"y ~ 0 + Intercept"
AIC_list<-c()
AIC_best<-0
new<-"gr1"
for (i in seq(1,100,1)){
  print("                                          ")
  print("______________Next Covariate______________")
  print(new)
  form1<-formula(ori1)
  res5<-inla(form1,data=inla.stack.data(stk.est,spde=spde),family=fam1,Ntrials=ntt,control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.est),compute=TRUE,link=1),control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE))
  AIC_list<-c(AIC_list,res5$waic$waic)
  if (i==1){
    AIC_best<-res5$waic$waic
  }
  if (i > 1 & AIC_best-res5$waic$waic>2){
    ori<-ori1
    AIC_best<-res5$waic$waic
  }else{
    print(paste0("!!Covariate    ",get(new),"    not used!!"))
  }
  print(AIC_list)
  print(ori)
  new<-paste0("gr",i)
  ori1<-paste(ori,get(new),sep = " + ")
  print("_________________DONE__________________")
  print("                                          ")
}

form1<-formula(ori)
res5<-inla(form1,data=inla.stack.data(stk.est,spde=spde),family=fam1,Ntrials=ntt,control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.est),compute=TRUE,link=1),control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE))
Efxplot(res5)
```

Thanks!
Chen Yangkang

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Extremely high slope estimate for one covariate
parts:
I would guess this is caused by bad (or no) scaling or standardization
mostly caused by the observations. covariates should be
scaled/standarized itself, for the same reason but also that without it
you do not control the effect of the priors.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Extremely high slope estimate for one covariate
parts:
no idea. but using bot 'x' and 'log(x+1)' as covariate, you are kind of
asking for a compromise, as you can write this as

beta1 * x + beta2 * log(1+x) = beta2 * (x + w * log(1+x))

for some weight 'w'. hence you ask, implicitely, to fine the weight 'w'
that makes the 'best covariate', and the sign of w might be negative,
hence the best covariate is some contrast between x and log(1+x).

just a guess
